text:
A: Hiya. Can you hear me alright?
B: Yeah, I can hear you. Alright. I'm Darren.
A: Oh, that's my husband's name! Sorry. I'm Joanne.
B: Ha. And my partner's Gemma, and I've just had a Gemma. Everyone's called the same thing today.
A: I've had a Gemma as well! Student nurse, in London?
B: Same one. Small study, this.
A: It is. Erm, so what do you do, Darren?
B: Warehouse. Picking and loading at a distribution centre off the M1, Sutton-in-Ashfield way. Fifty-odd hours a week. I clocked your shift calendar in your picture, all the coloured pens. Thought, she's on shifts and all.
A: Yeah, that's the rota. I'm a senior care assistant at a home near Huntingdon. I run the day shift. Different colour for each of us, otherwise Darren never knows when I'm in. My Darren, I mean.
B: Gemma's a carer. She'd love a calendar like that. Ours is just a scribbled thing on the fridge.
A: I've got a whiteboard on the fridge with the dinners on. Spag bol Monday, chicken pie Tuesday. Sounds sad, but with twelve-hour shifts you've got to.
B: No, that's sense. We just stand there at seven going "what we having for tea" and end up with a cob and chips.
A: A cob! Is that a roll?
B: Yeah, a cob. What do you call it?
A: A roll. Just a roll. Erm, I saw the dog treats on your... no, sorry, they're on mine. Have you got a dog?
B: Mabel. Staffie cross, about twelve. Snores like a lorry.
A: No! I've got a staffie. Bella. She's got a dodgy hip now, she doesn't like the river walk as much.
B: Mabel's the same, back legs have gone a bit. It's more of a shuffle than a walk. She still goes mad for a gravy bone, mind.
A: They all do. Is that a drawing behind you, on the wall?
B: Yeah, pit headstock. Old one near us. My grandad worked down there. I sketch a bit, buildings mostly.
A: You did that? That's really good, to be honest. You should be doing something with that, not a warehouse.
B: Erm, yeah. Did a year of art at college then packed it in for money. I've thought about tattoo work but I reckon I'm too old now. Forty.
A: No, that's rubbish. Forty's nothing. I'm forty-five and I'm doing a leadership diploma, the home's paying. You're never too old to learn something, you know.
B: Maybe. Do you like it, the course?
A: It's slow. I do it on my days off. I want deputy manager when ours retires, just deputy, mind, not the top job. Too much stress.
B: Fair. I'd do team leader for the money, but I'd only end up arguing with the managers. They time our breaks to the minute.
A: They don't! That's awful. Mind you, I'm the one who has a go when the young ones are late off their break. Sorry, am I the baddie now?
B: Ha. Depends if you're stood over them with a scanner.
A: No, I just give them a look. Gemma's on a home as well, you said? Is she alright with it?
B: Her back's bad. Lifting. The nurse girl said she wants to see her GP if it goes down her leg.
A: Yeah, she's right. Tell her to put it in writing to her manager and all, so it's on record. That's what I'd—
